lines.note: Tobishisari, tobishisaru, tobishisatta means leaping backwards or retreating with a jump. The damaged initial is T, matching the preceding page's catchword and the surviving headword, rather than OCR C; tor- begins Portuguese tornar.
Nar completes tornar, giving 'turn back' or 'go backwards'. The worn second word reads atras, not OCR airas; the weak t is supported by its stem and the motion described above.
Tooboo is explained by higashi no kata, 'the eastern direction'. The Portuguese names the east or Orient; the two printed long-o marks are retained independently.
Oriente completes the eastward-direction gloss. This short italic continuation is indented and remains a separate physical row.
Tobokashii denotes something uncertain or doubtful. The first vowel is damaged but rounded; the subsequent examples support Tobocaxij rather than OCR Tubocaxij.

The gloss specifies something that causes apprehension and concern. The verb is cauſa, not OCR canſa; the repeated adjective begins the negative example that continues below. The repeated adjective’s final ij is badly abraded; faint residual strokes and the complete form below support the incorporated reading.

runs.text: mo nai, l, tobocaxij cotoga nai.

lines.note: Tobokashii mo nai, alternatively tobokashii koto ga nai, expresses that there is nothing to fear or doubt. The Portuguese translation begins with Não ha and continues onto the next row.
Completes the negative example: there is nothing to fear or doubt. Recear and duuidar express apprehension and uncertainty, matching the adjective above.
Toboke, tobokeru, toboketa means dissembling or feigning something. The middle principal part clearly ends uru, correcting OCR ura; al- continues as algũa below.
Completes algũa couſa and introduces toboketa koto wo moosu, saying feigned or dissembling things. The long vowel in mǒſu is marked by the printed caron.

runs.text: Dizer couſas fingidas, ou com dißimulação.

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the Japanese example as saying fictitious things or speaking with dissimulation. Dißimulação preserves the printed double-s sort.
Soratoboke wo suru is feigning ignorance or speaking evasively. The visible paragraph sign introduces this further example; diſ- begins Portuguese dissimulação across the row boundary.

runs.text: ſimulação falando aßino ar, ou de maneira que

lines.note: Completes dissimulação, explaining an evasive, seemingly casual way of speaking. Falando replaces garbled OCR falanco; the damaged initial letters of ſimulação remain supported by their visible strokes and the split diſ- above. Printed aßino ar is retained without modernizing the spacing.
The final clause says that the speech is not understood, completing the description of evasiveness rather than beginning another entry.
Tobokemono denotes a feigning or dissembling person. The small final stop visible after the Portuguese adjective closes this independent entry.
Toboso is a poetic word for doors set on pivots or hinges, hence portas de couceira. P. is the poetic-use label; the divided Tobo- begins the example below.
Toboso wo hiraku means opening these doors. The leading ſouo completes Tobo- from the preceding physical row rather than constituting a separate word.

runs.text: Arroz vermelho. No Cami ſe diz

lines.note: Tooboshi is glossed as red rice. The following Portuguese sentence introduces the corresponding Cami-region name; the headword’s printed caron is preserved.
Taitogome completes “in Cami it is called ...”, supplying the regional rice-name rather than an independent example. The worn medial letters are retained from the visible form.
Toboshi, tobosu, toboita is lighting a lamp or fire. The historical principal part oita is printed and is not modernized; lu- continues as lume below.
Completes lume and gives hi wo tobosu, lighting a fire. Matsubi wo begins another example concerning a pine torch, continued on the next line.

Matsubi wo tobosu, alternatively akasu, means lighting a torch or pine splints. The abraded alternative is read acaſu: its surviving tall stroke and the lighting context support long ſ rather than OCR i. Most of that letter is lost, so the incorporated acaſu remains a nonblocking contextual reading.
De pinho specifies pinewood for the torch or splints. This short continuation closes the lighting entry.
Toboshii means poor, lacking, or in need. The printed paragraph sign introduces a phrase about presenting an appearance of poverty; Tobo- is divided from xij below.
Toboshii tei de gozaru describes an appearance or condition of want. The Portuguese “manner or appearance of” continues into the nouns on the next row.

runs.text: pobreza, & falta, ou mingoa. ¶ Itẽ, per

lines.note: Poverty, lack, and shortage complete the preceding example. Item, per met. introduces an extended figurative use across the line boundary; the printed abbreviation Itẽ is retained.
The figurative extension of toboshii is “to be hungry”. Ter fome is wholly italic Portuguese; OCR had incorrectly left its initial T outside the italic span.
Toboshisa is the noun formed from toboshii, denoting scarcity or need. The visibly short derivative ends in ſa with a following stop; OCR added a spurious final i.
Toboshū is the adverbial form associated with toboshii. Its final long-u mark is a caron; this short derivative receives no separate Portuguese gloss.

Toboshitsure, toboshitsururu, toboshitsureta describes several people carrying lights together. The Portuguese phrase is divided at the end of the row before tos below; the headword retains its historical ruru form. The dotted remnant before ũ- is incorporated as iũ- (juntos across the break); its stem is almost lost, so i versus j remains uncertain.

runs.text: tos candeas, ou tochas aceſas. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the account of carrying burning lamps or torches together. The Japanese example begins Tede-, continued by ni on the next row; its T is roman, correcting the OCR span boundary.

Tedeni taimatçuuo toboxitçure describes carrying lit torches in company, in the hands. The ç in the repeated verb is visible and restores the same tsure form as the headword; mui- continues as muitos.

runs.text: tos de companhia fachas aceſas nas mãos.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the example as many people together carrying burning torches in their hands. The line is a continuation, not a new definition.

runs.text: Filho deſta molher de agora. Vt,

lines.note: Toobuku means a child of the present wife, as the Portuguese explicitly explains. The long-o caron is retained rather than inferred from a modern spelling.
Kare wa toobuku ja identifies someone as a child of the current wife. The example’s vowel mark is read as the same downward caron as in the headword; mo- continues Portuguese molher below.
Completes molher de agora, “the present wife”, finishing the explanation of the child’s parentage. The printed molher spelling is retained.

Toobun is explained by sashiataru bun, the share due to someone. The damaged initial is a capital T rather than OCR r. The gloss is about a person’s allotted portion, distinct from the equal-measure sense below.

runs.text: alguem como ſe repartißem por algũs tantas

lines.note: The share is illustrated by distributing a number of prayers among several people. Repartißem, supported by the printed double-s sort, corrects OCR repartipem; the sentence continues below. The middle s-sort is worn, so the ß representation remains a nonblocking typographic caveat.
The prayers complete the distribution example. Toobun tsukamatsutta states that the speaker performed the allotted share; the printed principal verb form remains historical.

runs.text: Fiz, ou compri com o que me coube.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains that the speaker did or fulfilled what fell to him. Compri is the printed spelling and is not silently modernized to cumpri.

runs.text: Igualdade no peſo, medida, ou quã-

lines.note: This separate toobun entry means equality of weight, measure, or quantity. Its upward circumflex differs visibly from the preceding allocated-share entry’s caron.
Tidade completes quãtidade, quantity. The short indented row belongs entirely to the equality definition.
Toobunna is the adjectival form, equal in weight and measure. The large initial has the damaged right arm of T, not the F supplied by OCR.
Toobunni is labelled adverbial. The example toobunni yaru, alternatively watasu on the next row, describes giving or handing over in equal quantity.

runs.text: Dar, ou entregar da meſma mane-

lines.note: Watasu completes the alternative verb. The Portuguese states “give or hand over in the same manner”; a visible small line-end hyphen after mane- is retained.
Ira completes maneira, followed by “or in equal quantity”. This closes the adverbial equality entry.

Toburai denotes burial, funeral rites, or another commendation for the dead. The damaged ending reads ai, not OCR -i; the unindented headword begins an entry whose Portuguese definition continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: mendação que ſe faz por de functo.

lines.note: Mendação completes cõ-mendação from the previous column: a commendation performed for a deceased person. The cedilla is visible, correcting OCR mendaſão; the printed spacing de functo is retained.
Toburai, toburǒ, toburǒta gives the verb for performing funeral rites or commending someone’s soul. En- begins encomendar on the next row.
The Portuguese completes the commendation of someone’s soul. Hito no ato introduces the Japanese example; its printed stop and divided continuation are retained.

The example continues with an alternative involving gose, the afterlife, and toburǒ, to commemorate the dead. The damaged verb begins to-, not OCR tu-. The printed goxeno is retained rather than silently changing its particle to an expected uo. The vowel immediately after t in toburǒ and the consonant in goxeno are abraded, so these retained choices remain nonblocking reading caveats.

A separate sense of toburau is visiting someone or asking after them. The third principal part visibly has a single grave accent, òta, unlike the caron in the preceding entry; this printed difference is preserved. Per- begins the Portuguese verb perguntar.

runs.text: gũtar por elle: cõmummẽte ſe vſa nos liuros.

lines.note: Completes perguntar and states that this usage is common in books. Liuros is the historical livros spelling; the visible i missing from OCR luros is restored.
Tokaku is an adverb equated with tomokakumo. Adu. supplies the grammatical label, while i introduces the explanatory equivalent. The Portuguese gloss begins “in whatever manner”.

runs.text: maneira que ſeia, ou em todo caſo, ou de hũa

lines.note: Continues the possibilities: in whatever manner, in any case, or in one manner. The heavily abraded ſeia is read from the surviving long ſ, faint vowel position, and dotted i; it remains a nonblocking weak-glyph reading rather than being modernized to seja.

runs.text: maneira, ou de outra. ¶ Com verbos ne-

lines.note: Completes “in one manner or another”. The paragraph then introduces the special interpretation with negative verbs, divided ne- / gatiuos.
With negative verbs, tokaku means “in no way”. Gatiuos completes negatiuos; the visible t corrects OCR gariuos without changing the historical spelling.
Tokage is a lizard, directly glossed lagartixa. The headword’s gue supplies the voiced ge syllable.
Tokagiri is identified as the same animal in Ximo. Ximo is a regional name embedded in Portuguese explanation, not part of the headword or a Japanese example.
Tookai is explained as higashi no umi, the eastern sea. The Portuguese gives the eastward sea relative to Miaco, whose name appears on the next physical row.
Completes respeito do Miaco: east is reckoned with reference to the capital. Miaco is an embedded Japanese place designation within the Portuguese gloss.
Tokai is crossing the sea, explicitly explained by umi wo wataru. The damaged initial T replaces OCR r; the unmarked vowel belongs to this separate entry and is not assimilated to Tôcai above.
Completes nauegar, sailing, and gives tokai suru as the example. The Japanese phrase stays roman after italic Vt.
Tookaidoo is glossed literally as higashi no umi no michi, the eastern-sea road. The first long-o circumflex and final caron are separately visible and preserved.

runs.text: ou caminho da parte do Leſte, ou caminho por

lines.note: The Portuguese defines the eastern route or road and begins an alternative description of a route by sea. This is continuing explanation of Tôcaidǒ.

runs.text: mar, ou ao longo do mar do Leſte em reſpeito

lines.note: The route may be by sea or along the eastern sea; the phrase “in relation to” continues onto the following row.
Do Miaco identifies the capital as the reference point for this eastern route. The place designation completes the Portuguese sentence.
Tookan is equated with naozari, something casual, indifferent, or ordinary. The historical Nauozari spelling is preserved; the explanation develops a negative construction below.

runs.text: ou menos, ou ordinaria. Vſaſe eſta palaura cõ-

lines.note: Completes the sense “more or less” or ordinary, then introduces the word’s common use. The divided Portuguese cõ- remains italic, including its printed hyphen.

runs.text: mummẽte com negatiuo pera moſtrar amizade

lines.note: With a negative, tookan expresses close friendship. The u in mummẽte and the t in moſtrar are supported by the scan, correcting OCR mammẽte and moſirar.

runs.text: eſtreita, & que não he ordinaria com alguem.

lines.note: The friendship is close and not merely ordinary. This explains why denying casualness conveys intimacy rather than estrangement.
Tookan mo nai hito de gozaru describes a person with whom one is closely familiar. The Portuguese “he is a man” is divided at ho-.

runs.text: mem com quem corro familiarmente, & me cõ-

lines.note: Mem completes homem; the speaker associates familiarly with the person and communicates with him. Familiarmente corrects OCR familtarmente; cõ- starts the next divided verb.

Munico completes cõmunico, “I communicate much”. A further Japanese expression about speaking together familiarly begins; the printed Tôcannǒ form is retained rather than reconstructed from a modern idiom.
Ru completes awasuru. The Portuguese renders the expression as dealing and communicating familiarly; familiar- continues onto the following row.
Completes familiarmente, then gives the adjectival alternatives tookanna and tookan-gamashii. The next Portuguese definition starts Eſ- and continues across the line.
Tar completes estar: to be on less familiar terms in a friendship. This positive adjective contrasts with the negative construction expressing intimacy above.
Tokko is explained as an implement of religious practice, okonai no doogu. The Portuguese begins its description as a metal instrument.

The metal implement is used by Buddhist monks in their prayers and ceremonies. The entire printed Bõzos is upright, correcting the OCR boundary that isolated only B; it is a Portuguese lexical form rather than a Japanese typeface-toggle term.
Cações completes deprecações, prayers or supplications, followed by ceremonies. This finishes the ritual-implement definition.

runs.text: Fruita aßi chamada, como bolotas: to-

lines.note: Tochi is a fruit compared with acorns. The gloss provides an analogy, not enough evidence by itself to impose a botanical species identification; to- begins tomaſe.
The word also denotes the tree producing that fruit. The printed pella and aruore are preserved historical spellings.
Tochigane are iron rings for tethering horses. The definition continues to specify the location on the next row; gane is the metal-related element.
The horses are tied in the stable. This completes the iron-ring definition rather than introducing another use of the fruit-name tochi.

runs.text: Arroz, ou comer feito da quella

lines.note: Tochi ii is cooked food made from the previously named tochi fruit. The scan’s word separation and iy spelling are retained rather than converted to a modern form.
Fruita Tochi completes the food description, naming its ingredient. Tochi is embedded within the Portuguese gloss and can be marked for whole-word typeface review.
Tochimeki, tochimeku, tochimeita means being restless or flustered. The eita principal part is retained as historical morphology, not expanded to a modernized conjugation.

runs.text: apreßado como quando hum ſe ve ſobreſalteado

lines.note: The Portuguese describes a hurried, agitated state when one finds oneself suddenly alarmed. The following row supplies the causes of the alarm.

runs.text: de inimigos na guerra, ou com o fogo poſto na

lines.note: The examples are attack by enemies in war or a fire set in the house. The location na continues into caſa on the next row.
Completes “in the house” and gives tochi-tochi to suru as an equivalent expression for the flustered state. The repetition is part of the Japanese example, followed by italic Idem.

Tochimekashi, tochimekasu, tochimekaita is the causative counterpart, making someone hurry or become agitated. Its printed beginning is flush with the headword margin, so the provisional continuation indentation is removed.
Guem completes alguem, and the gloss adds moving about in confusion or perturbation. It remains an indented continuation of the causative entry.

runs.text: Hũa laya de Mochis feitos da

lines.note: Tochi mochi are a kind of cakes made from the tochi fruit. The entry starts at the headword margin; Mochis occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is a whole-word typeface-review candidate.

The ingredient is the fruit named Tochi. The small damaged capital is T, not OCR I; the word remains part of the Portuguese description, and the isolated text below is a catchword rather than another body row.
